dedupe_keys.name: puerto rico after hurricane maria satellite nighttime lights assessment of electricity restoration

description: This study used daily satellite nighttime lights to estimate where and for how long Puerto Rico lost electricity after Hurricane Maria in September 2017, the longest blackout in US history, and to track restoration across all of the island's settlements. Miguel Román, Eleanor Stokes and colleagues at NASA Goddard, the Universities Space Research Association and partner institutions published it in PLOS ONE in June 2019, linking outage and recovery times to census characteristics of residents. Lights fell by 80 percent right after the storm; long outages of more than 120 days hit 41 percent of rural municipalities against 29 percent of urban ones, concentrated in northern and eastern districts, and within cities poorer residents in less dense detached housing waited longest because restoration there lagged. The estimates are independent of utility data and include off-grid supply. Format and access: open access article with figures and methods. Licence: the article is free of all copyright; free. Caveats: lights are a proxy for power, and clouds and moonlight limit daily observations. It gives a method and benchmark for resilience and hazard exposure studies of power restoration and its equity. Related catalogue records are NASA Black Marble and the World Bank Black Marble packages.
